synopsis: HMI is a safety-critical part of collision mitigation: warnings can fail if operators do not notice, understand or trust them, and the interface determines whether staged intervention leaves real time to respond [f11824, f11843]. The University of Queensland’s ACARP C24028 project ran in 2017 with follow-on work to 2019; its modified haul-truck simulator provided the strongest haul-truck-specific human-interface evidence found, with a richer proximity display reducing collision risk, braking force and travel time, but the project addressed advisory interfaces rather than automatic braking [f3314, f3315, f3468, f3466, f573]. ISO 16001:2017 requires audible warnings at least 3 dB above ambient under specified operating conditions, visual warnings within a forward 120° arc, a flashing red light for the most severe warning, and no haptic-only warnings; ISO 21815-3 requires distinguishable warning levels [f2406, f2408, f2410, f6240]. Nuisance and ambiguous indications remain material risks: continuous haul-truck audible warnings were annoying enough to be switched off, an 18% false-alarm result does not establish an acceptable lower rate, and WorkSafe SIR 286 links recovery problems to mode misunderstanding and desensitization [f11840, f3331, f10719, f10839]. Operator studies should precede expensive prototype safety tests, VIL can exercise the real interface alongside braking dynamics without exposing people or targets, and recordings must capture operator inputs and warning states to assess usefulness [f13415, f13393, f5636, f5637]. Haptic effectiveness remains an explicit research gap, despite on-road provisions allowing very brief brake-jerk cues above 4 m/s²; degraded modes, annunciation, recovery procedures and human understanding therefore need explicit validation [f5837, f6498, f11035].
